Nirantar Flow: Two Hundred and Fourteen Logos

A Bengaluru integration platform has 214 enterprise customers, 18,400 paid seats and about 61,000 humans who touch its software every month. Its head of product has to tell the board on Monday morning which of those three numbers the company is actually run on — and the more he looks, the less he believes any of them.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 13 September 2026, Ashwin Bhide was sitting at his dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two laptops open and a printed board pre-read face down beside them. The pre-read was eleven pages. Page four had been rewritten nine times since Wednesday and was, at that moment, wrong again.

Ashwin was Vice-President of Product at Nirantar Data Systems, whose platform, Nirantar Flow, moved data and ran automated workflows between the systems that large Indian and Gulf enterprises actually used — SAP and Oracle instances, Tally, Salesforce, core banking systems, GST filing utilities, warehouse-management tools, and an increasing number of internal services that nobody had documented. The board met at half past nine on Monday morning at the company's Prestige Tech Park office, and item two on the agenda read: Metric of record — product and commercial alignment ahead of Series C.

The phrase "metric of record" had come from Sunita Rege, Nirantar's co-founder and chief executive, and it had come with a reason. In the preceding financial year the product team had reported a 34 per cent rise in weekly active seats; the revenue team had reported 41 per cent growth in seats sold; customer success had reported a 92 per cent gross renewal rate by logo. All three had been true. Net revenue retention had come in at 104 per cent, against a plan of 128. Nine accounts had not renewed. Seven of the nine had been sitting in the green band of the account health score on the day they gave notice, and two of those seven had been quoted in Nirantar's own marketing in the same quarter.

What Ashwin had spent the weekend on was not the board's question. It was a smaller one that had started to look larger. On Friday afternoon Ritwik Bose, the company's senior data scientist, had sent him a two-line message from Toronto: Before Monday, ask engineering when telemetry from VPC deployments last landed. I think the answer is April. Ashwin had asked. The answer was 14 April. It was now September.

2. How Nirantar got here

Nirantar Data Systems was founded in Pune in 2018 by Sunita Rege and Farhan Qureshi, who had spent nine years together building integration middleware inside a large Indian IT services firm and had grown tired of watching the same three-month connector project repeated at every client. Their premise was that Indian enterprises, unlike their American counterparts, would not buy a self-service developer tool on a credit card; they would buy a platform, with a contract, a named implementation partner and a support SLA — but the people inside those enterprises who actually built things would abandon anything that felt like enterprise software.

The company grew accordingly. By September 2026 it had 214 paying accounts, ₹112 crore of annual recurring revenue, and offices in Bengaluru, Pune, Singapore, Dubai and a small sales presence in Edison, New Jersey. Roughly 71 per cent of ARR came from India, 18 per cent from the Gulf and the balance from South-East Asia and a handful of North American logos.

One decision, taken in March 2021, constrains almost everything the company can do today. Nirantar's second-largest prospect at the time, a Mumbai private bank, refused to allow workflow metadata to leave its own cloud tenancy. Rather than lose the deal, Farhan agreed to ship a customer-hosted edition: the full Nirantar runtime, deployed inside the customer's own VPC, with a lightweight telemetry agent that would report aggregate counters back to Nirantar. The deal closed at ₹1.9 crore. The architecture that came with it never went away. By 2026, 47 of 214 accounts — 23 per cent of logos, and because they skewed large, 39 per cent of ARR — ran in customer-hosted mode. The telemetry agent had been treated, in Farhan's own later phrase, as "a nice-to-have written by an intern in a hurry". It broke quietly whenever a customer tightened an egress rule, and nobody was paged when it did.

A second consequence of 2021 was commercial. To make the customer-hosted edition saleable, Nirantar priced it on named seats — a builder licence at ₹1.42 lakh per year, and a cheaper operator licence at ₹38,000 — because a consumption meter inside someone else's VPC was a conversation the company did not want to have in 2021. Seats became the shape of every contract, every quota and every commission plan that followed.

3. The industry around it

Nirantar sold into an Indian enterprise market that had been rewired twice in a decade, and both rewirings created work for an integration platform. GST e-invoicing had obliged every mid-sized manufacturer and distributor to push structured data out of systems that had never been asked to produce it. The account aggregator framework, UPI and the settlement rails around NPCI had made financial-services customers dependent on machine-to-machine flows that ran continuously rather than nightly. ONDC had pulled retailers and logistics providers into catalogue and order integrations they had not planned for. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose rules had been phased in through 2025 and 2026, had made every one of Nirantar's customers newly careful about what left their premises — including, awkwardly, product telemetry.

Its competition came from three directions. Global platforms — the integration suites sold by the large cloud vendors, and specialist workflow tools — competed on capability and lost on price and on data-residency comfort. Indian software companies with strong SME distribution, Zoho above all, competed from below with integration bundled into suites the customer already owned. And the Indian systems integrators — Infosys, TCS, Wipro and the mid-tier firms — competed sideways, by offering to build the same flows as a service, billed by the person-month. Freshworks and Postman were quoted constantly in Nirantar's investor conversations as proof that Indian product companies could sell globally at software margins; both were also quoted, less helpfully, as examples of companies that knew exactly what their unit of usage was.

The Gulf exposure mattered out of proportion to its size. Qasr Industrial Group, a Dubai conglomerate with construction-materials, logistics and facilities businesses across the Emirates, Oman and Saudi Arabia, had signed in June 2023 and now paid ₹4.62 crore a year — Nirantar's largest single contract, 4.1 per cent of ARR, renewable on 31 December 2026. The contract fixed the builder-seat price in dirhams until 2028 and contained a most-favoured-customer clause on list pricing. Any move away from seat-based pricing had to survive a conversation with Qasr's group CIO first.

4. What happened, and what turned out not to be true

The sequence that brought Ashwin to his dining table began in February 2025, when Nirantar shipped the second version of its account health score. Version one had been a spreadsheet maintained by customer success. Version two was a model: Ritwik Bose, working from Toronto, fitted a gradient-boosted classifier on 41 accounts with known renewal outcomes, using eleven features — weekly active builder seats, flows in production, connector diversity, support-ticket volume, executive-sponsor changes, invoice ageing and five usage ratios. It scored every account weekly from 0 to 100 and bucketed them green, amber and red. It was, by the measure everyone applied to it, an immediate success: over the following six quarters, 94 per cent of green accounts renewed and 62 per cent of red accounts either churned or contracted.

Three things were believed through 2025 that are no longer safe to believe. The first was that seats measured value. The seat count had grown 41 per cent; what nobody had decomposed until August 2026 was that 58 per cent of net new seats in the year had come from four enterprise agreements in which seats were bundled — sold as a block of 250 or 500 "platform seats" at a steep discount, to make a total contract value land at a round number. Those seats were provisioned in Nirantar's licence system on the day the contract was signed. Whether anyone logged in was a separate question, and one nobody's compensation depended on.

The second was that the health score predicted renewals. In February 2025 the score had been given an override field, so that a customer-success manager who knew something the model did not could move an account between bands. By mid-2026, 31 per cent of all account-weeks carried an override. Ritwik's retrospective, delivered on 4 September, established that the median override was applied eleven days after the renewal conversation had opened in the CRM. The model had not been predicting renewals; to a substantial degree it had been recording them.

The third was that the numbers described the whole business. The telemetry agent in customer-hosted deployments had stopped reporting on 14 April 2026, after a routine certificate rotation. Until 11 September, every dashboard in the company had been computed on the 167 cloud-hosted accounts and had silently treated the other 47 as having no activity to report — which, in the health score, is indistinguishable from an account that has gone quiet. Customer success had been overriding those accounts to green for five months, correctly, on the evidence of their own eyes.

Meanwhile a fourth thread had been running. In April 2026, under pressure from the finance team to show usage-linked growth, Sunita had asked Ashwin to model consumption pricing: charging for successful flow runs rather than for seats. The model was built for the top twelve accounts. It suggested that the same customers would pay 19 per cent more in aggregate, and that the distribution would change violently — three accounts would pay roughly double, five rather less. That model is Exhibit 6, and it is the reason the metric question could not be postponed: if Nirantar were to bill on runs, then seats would become, within eighteen months, a number with no commercial meaning at all.

5. The people

Sunita Rege, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. She wants one account-level number in the board deck and she wants it to survive diligence for a Series C round being negotiated at a valuation of ₹1,340 crore. Her stated position is that Nirantar should report "activated accounts" — accounts that have crossed a defined threshold of real production use — because that is what a sophisticated investor will interrogate. What she does not say aloud is that she has already shown a slide with 71 per cent activation on it to two prospective investors, using the definition in Exhibit 2, column A.

Hardik Shah, Chief Revenue Officer, Edison, New Jersey. Fourteen years selling Indian software into North America, and the architect of the platform-seat bundle. His position is that seats are the only metric the field can sell, forecast and be paid on, and that changing the unit of account eight weeks before the close of the Qasr renewal is professional self-harm. His incentive is explicit: 40 per cent of his variable compensation is tied to net new seats. What he does not say is that he agrees with Ritwik about the bundles, and has quietly told two of his enterprise reps to stop selling them from October.

Priya Nambiar, VP Customer Success, Singapore. Runs 19 CSMs covering India, the Gulf and South-East Asia. Her position is that any health score built only on product telemetry will be worse than her team's judgement, and she has five months of correct overrides to prove it. Her incentive is a renewal-rate target that her overrides help her manage. What she does not say is that her team's override guidance, circulated internally in October 2025, explicitly instructs CSMs to move an account to green once a renewal is "verbally confirmed".

Farhan Qureshi, co-founder and VP Engineering, Pune. His position is that no metric decision should be taken until instrumentation is rebuilt: a single event taxonomy, an owner for every metric, and a telemetry agent with an alert on it. He has costed the rebuild at ₹2.4 crore and fourteen weeks. What he does not say is that the 2021 architecture was his decision, that he knew the agent was fragile, and that a monitoring ticket for it has been carried in his backlog since November 2024.

Ritwik Bose, senior data scientist, Toronto. He wrote the health score and then wrote the paper that discredited it. His position is that Nirantar should stop scoring accounts and start measuring teams: the unit that adopts or abandons Nirantar, he argues, is not the legal entity but the individual business team inside it that owns a set of flows. What he does not say — though his memo hints at it — is that his teams analysis is possible for only 88 of 214 accounts, because the rest do not tag their workspaces.

Marta Brenner, principal designer, Berlin. Her position is that the company's entire user model is wrong, because the humans who get value from Nirantar mostly never open it: they receive a reconciliation file, approve an exception in Microsoft Teams, or see a WhatsApp alert when a flow fails. Counting logins, she argues, counts the wrong people. What she does not say is that the redesign her team has scoped for the next two quarters is justified in its brief by weekly-active-seat growth, the very metric she is arguing against.

Sneha Kamath, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. Her position is that whatever the product organisation measures must reconcile to revenue within one rupee, because the Series C data room will contain both. She is not especially attached to seats; she is attached to auditability. What she does not say is that her FY26 NRR of 104 per cent was computed excluding the four bundle accounts, on the grounds that they were "structurally anomalous", and that this exclusion is documented only in a footnote of a working file.

Yousef Haddad, Group CIO, Qasr Industrial Group, Dubai. Not a Nirantar employee, but present in every conversation. His position, stated in a call on 2 September, is that Qasr will renew if Nirantar can show that the platform has reduced his integration headcount, and that he does not care how many of his people log in. His incentive is a group-level cost reduction target for 2027. What he does not say is that Qasr's own internal IT team has begun evaluating an open-source alternative for two of its four business units.

7. Voices

"Every board deck for three years has opened with logos and seats. If page one now opens with 'activated accounts, 44 per cent', the first question is what it was last year, and the honest answer is that we do not know, because the definition did not exist. I am not against the number. I am against discovering it in public."

Sneha Kamath, CFO, in the pre-read review call, 10 September 2026

"Please stop saying the model was wrong. The model was fine. It learnt the thing we fed it, which was our own opinion about which accounts would renew, arriving eleven days after we had formed that opinion. If you want a model that predicts renewals, you have to stop telling it the answer."

Ritwik Bose, Toronto, in #metrics-wg on Slack, 4 September, 02:41 IST

"My CSMs overrode 47 accounts to green between April and August. Every one of those overrides was correct. The platform was running fine; the pipe carrying the numbers was broken. You are now proposing to build a scorecard that would have called all 47 of them at risk and sent me into 47 renewal conversations apologising for a problem that did not exist."

Priya Nambiar, Singapore, e-mail to Ashwin Bhide and Sunita Rege, 11 September

"Question from my side, maybe naive. In the Pune plant flow, forty-one people get an exception mail every morning and nine of them act on it. None of them has a seat. In our numbers that account has one user. In the customer's mind it has fifty. Whose count are we managing to?"

Marta Brenner, Berlin, in the product review, 8 September

"I can rebuild the instrumentation properly in fourteen weeks for ₹2.4 crore and I will put my name on it. What I cannot do is rebuild history. Whatever we announce on Monday, the first clean quarter of data is January."

Farhan Qureshi, Pune, WhatsApp to Ashwin, 12 September

"We are not measuring how many of my people use your system. I am measuring whether I still need eleven integration developers in 2027. Show me that and the renewal is a formality. Show me a login chart and I will forward it to procurement, which is not where you want it to go."

Yousef Haddad, Group CIO, Qasr Industrial Group, Dubai, call transcript, 2 September

8. The options as Ashwin sees them

Page four of the pre-read sets out three choices, and Ashwin has begun to distrust the fact that they are three.

Option A — the activated account. Adopt definition B from Exhibit 2 as the company's account-level North Star: an account is activated when it runs three or more flows in production and has five or more weekly-active builder seats. Rebuild the health score from behaviour only, with overrides removed. Report activated accounts, and activation rate within 90 days of go-live, at every board meeting. The attraction is that it puts product and customer success on the same target. The difficulty is that 39 per cent of ARR cannot be measured against it until January, that Priya's team loses a tool that has been keeping them honest, and that the "five weekly-active seats" clause would classify Qasr — which runs enormous volume through a small central team — as not activated.

Option B — the run. Move the company's centre of gravity to consumption: report monthly successful production flow runs as the North Star, with runs per account as the account-level cut, and accelerate the pricing transition so that commercial and product metrics converge. The attraction is that runs are the thing customers actually buy value from and the thing a machine can count without asking a human. The difficulty is Exhibit 6: the transition redistributes revenue violently, it cannot begin with Qasr before 2028, and a metric that rewards volume will reward inefficient flows, of which Nirantar has many.

Option C — fix the pipes first. Announce no new metric of record. Commit Farhan's ₹2.4 crore and fourteen weeks, instrument properly, and bring a proposal back in January with a full quarter of clean data behind it. The attraction is intellectual honesty. The difficulty is that the Series C process will not wait, that Hardik's FY27 quota plan is due on 30 September and must be denominated in something, and that "we will tell you in January" is a sentence a board hears as an absence of a product leader.

What unsettles Ashwin about his own page is that all three options assume the account is the unit. Ritwik's memo argues that adoption happens at the level of a team inside an account, and that Nirantar has eleven accounts in which one division is thriving and three are dormant — a fact invisible in every exhibit above. Marta's argument is that the human unit is wrong too. And Sneha's objection is not really about which metric but about who owns it, how often it is published, and which decision it is allowed to change. None of those three arguments is an option on page four.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at 09:30 on Monday, 14 September 2026. The Series C term sheet is expected to be signed or abandoned by 31 October; the lead investor's diligence questionnaire, received on 8 September, asks for "product-qualified account definition and cohort activation curves, monthly, for eight quarters". Nirantar can supply four quarters, for 78 per cent of ARR, on a definition that did not exist until August.

The money is finite. The FY27 plan has ₹6.8 crore of discretionary spend; Farhan's instrumentation rebuild would take ₹2.4 crore of it and fourteen engineering weeks that are currently allocated to a connector roadmap sold into two Gulf deals. Priya has asked for four more CSMs at a fully loaded ₹58 lakh a year for the India-based roles and ₹1.1 crore for the Singapore ones — a salary asymmetry that has itself become an argument about where account health should be judged from.

The contracts bind. Qasr's seat price is fixed in dirhams until 2028 and carries a most-favoured-customer clause that would extend any published discount to them. Two Indian banking customers, 6.7 per cent of ARR between them, permit no product telemetry to leave their environments at all; under the DPDP Act their legal teams have become less flexible, not more. And Hardik's FY27 compensation plans must go to the sales organisation by 30 September, twelve working days after the board meeting, in whatever unit the company decides to measure.

10. Questions for discussion

1. In Exhibit 1, which of the six columns is the best single description of how much of Nirantar's product is being used, and what does each of the other five over- or understate?

2. Exhibit 2 shows that tighter activation definitions are associated with higher renewal rates. Explain precisely why this is not evidence that Nirantar should adopt the tightest definition.

3. Exhibits 3 and 4 disagree about whether the health score identifies risk. Reconstruct how each was produced, and state what you would need to see before trusting either.

4. If you were designing an account health score for Nirantar knowing what Exhibit 5 says about coverage, what would you measure, who would own each input, and at what cadence would it be allowed to change a decision?

5. Ritwik argues the unit of adoption is the team, not the account; Marta argues it is a person who never logs in; Yousef argues it is eleven integration developers he no longer needs. Can one measurement system serve all three, or must Nirantar choose? What is given up by each choice?

6. It is Monday morning. Ashwin has twenty minutes on the agenda and a pre-read the board has already read. What does he put on page four, what does he say about the five months of missing telemetry, and what does he commit the company to before 30 September?

Sunday, 11.50 p.m.

Ashwin turned the pre-read over and read page four again. The three options were still there, cleanly argued, each with its risks listed underneath in a smaller font. Beside them on the table was Ritwik's memo, eight pages, and a sheet on which Ashwin had written and rewritten a single sentence in an attempt to define what it meant for a customer to be getting value from Nirantar Flow. The current version read: An account is healthy when a named business team depends on at least one Nirantar flow to close a process it cannot close another way. He could not instrument it. He was not sure he could defend it in a data room. He was fairly sure it was true.

His phone lit up with a message from Hardik, who was eleven and a half hours behind in New Jersey and had just started his Sunday: Are we still telling them 18,400? Ashwin looked at it for a while, and then at the clock, and did not reply.

A reading case for experienced product and general managers

1. Two Rooms, Two Weeks Apart

On the morning of 11 February 2026, in a meeting room in Hyderabad's Financial District, Jyotika Menon was preparing to tell her board that Kalpavriksh Data Systems had grown revenue 34 percent year on year. Kalpavriksh sold Kalpavriksh Flow, a pipeline platform used by lenders, insurers and payment companies to pull records from core banking systems, account-aggregator feeds and card networks and land them, reconciled, in a warehouse. It was priced by consumption — per million rows moved, per pipeline-hour. There were no seats, and no login-based engagement curve worth plotting, because most humans who touched Flow touched it twice a quarter while the machines ran continuously.

The number that ruined the morning came from Devansh Kulkarni, her analyst in Bengaluru, asked for a routine decomposition of the top twenty accounts. Lalima Finance, a Mumbai NBFC paying ₹1.9 crore a year, drew 94 percent of its consumption from pipelines authored by one engineer, and that engineer had resigned in January. Nobody had noticed, because every dashboard Kalpavriksh kept was green and rising. Jyotika's problem was not a wrong metric but a measurement system that took the account as an undifferentiated meter reading — and a meter cannot tell you that the hand on the tap is leaving the building.

Eight days later and eight hundred kilometres away, Latika Deshpande faced the mirror image. Latika was VP Product at Lakshna Works in Pune, which sold Lakshna Field, a seat-licensed suite for field operations — work orders, crew scheduling, asset inspection — to large manufacturers, contractors and utilities: 240 enterprise accounts, ₹64 crore of ARR. Fourteen months earlier the company had built an account health score blending seat utilisation, weekly active users and support-ticket volume. On 19 February, Konkan Infra Projects — ₹2.6 crore of ARR, health score 82, comfortably green — issued a non-renewal notice effective 30 June.

Farida Qureshi, Lakshna's customer-success lead in Chennai, had the explanation within a day. Konkan had 1,400 provisioned seats, and weekly active users were high because the supervisors' app pushed a daily shift acknowledgement that every crew lead tapped through in four seconds. Meanwhile nobody in maintenance planning — the function that had justified the purchase — had built a preventive-maintenance schedule in seven months; after a failed data migration they had gone back to a spreadsheet. The score was measuring compliance with a notification and calling it adoption.

Jyotika was measuring an account as if it had no people in it; Latika was measuring people as if they added up to an account. Neither had decided, explicitly, what unit of value their product created, and for whom.

2. The Idea, and Who Disagrees About It

B2B product metrics is the practice of measuring value creation at the level of the organisation that pays, while keeping enough resolution below that level — by function, by workflow, by individual — to explain why the organisation's number is what it is. Four units sit in the stack: the account, the commercial entity that signs and is invoiced; entitlement, what the contract permits, whether seats or committed volume; provisioned use, entitlement actually handed out; and activation, the observable behaviour, validated against renewal outcomes, that marks where value begins to accrue. The practice is choosing these four definitions deliberately and always knowing which one a given number describes.

The problem it solves is older than SaaS. In the perpetual-licence era, vendors sold seats that were never installed — shelfware — and it scarcely mattered, because revenue was recognised at signature. Subscription pricing destroyed that insulation: when the customer can leave annually, the gap between purchase and use becomes the central commercial risk. The SaaS-metrics literature of roughly 2010 to 2013 supplied the financial layer — MRR, gross and net retention, cohort curves; the customer-success movement of the same period supplied the account health score; product-led-growth writing later in the decade supplied the individual activation curve, imported wholesale from consumer products. Three traditions, three functions, three questions, and the incoherence a product manager meets today is the residue of their collision.

Four positions can be stated sharply enough to be argued with.

The account-primacy school holds that the renewal is the only event that clears money, so every metric must roll up to an account. It will sign: a metric that cannot be attributed to a paying account does not belong on an executive dashboard. It will not sign: individual user behaviour is noise. The user-primacy school, native to bottom-up products, holds that accounts do not adopt — people do. It will sign: activation is an individual event, and the account's number is arithmetic on top of it. It will not sign: an account average can substitute for the distribution beneath it. The workflow school, strongest in vertical software, holds that the denominator is neither humans nor entities but units of work — shipments planned, invoices matched, inspections closed. It will sign: seats are a licensing artefact and a poor denominator for anything. It will not sign: a workflow metric can be read without knowing how many people produced it. The retention-primacy school, usually finance's, holds that net revenue retention is the only honest scoreboard. It will sign: an activation definition that does not separate renewing from churning cohorts is decoration. It will not sign: a product metric must be predictive before it can be useful for diagnosis.

Most practitioners are mixtures of all four, which is fine; most arguments in metric reviews are unacknowledged proxy fights between two of them, which is not.

3. Mechanics: Building the Stack, and What Breaks Underneath It

The stack looks trivial written down and is not, because each layer's definition carries second-order consequences.

Three steps are routinely left implicit, and all three were where Jyotika and Latika lost.

First, define the account against the invoice, then check it against the tenant. An account receives one contract and one invoice; product analytics counts tenants, the isolated workspaces the system provisions, and the two diverge constantly. Jamuna Steel Works ran seven tenants because each plant had onboarded separately: the CRM said one customer worth ₹4.1 crore, the product database seven averaging ₹59 lakh. Any metric computed per tenant and reported per account is wrong by a factor that varies by customer, which makes comparisons across the book meaningless in a way no error bar reveals.

Second, treat the activation definition as a hypothesis with a test. The test is discrimination against a known outcome — usually renewal twelve months out — and the temptation is to stop at whichever definition shows the biggest gap between groups. That criterion alone is wrong, as three candidate bars run against 240 Lakshna accounts showed.

They answer different questions — B is a triage threshold, C a definition of what good looks like — and forcing one definition to serve both yields a number too loose to steer by and too tight to trust.

Third, aggregate with an explicit rule, and rarely let it be the mean. An account has no activation rate; it has a distribution across functions. The aggregation choice — mean across users, share of functions clearing a bar, minimum across critical functions — is a policy decision that changes which accounts you look at. Konkan's mean-based score of 82 and its function-based score of 33 describe the same account.

For consumption products the analogous second-order quantity is concentration, worth making formal because the intuition is slippery. Take each account's usage, compute the share attributable to each human author, and sum the squares — the Herfindahl construction borrowed from industrial economics. Lalima's shares were 0.94, 0.04 and 0.02: concentration 0.886. Kartavya Lending, a Kochi account paying ₹40 lakh, had six authors at 0.31, 0.22, 0.18, 0.12, 0.10 and 0.07: concentration 0.206. On revenue Lalima was worth nearly five Kartavyas; on durability, less than one. Across the book, accounts above 0.70 were 38 percent of logos but 52 percent of revenue, and churned at 21 percent against 6 percent. More than half of Kalpavriksh's revenue rested on people rather than institutions.

4. The Conditions, Stated as Claims

The apparatus earns its cost only when four conditions hold, each testable.

Claim one: the payer and the user are different populations. True at Lakshna, where a procurement head signs and crew leads use; true at Kalpavriksh, where a CTO signs and engineers build. Where it fails — a two-person studio buying a ₹1,200-a-month tool — the account layer is ceremonial and individual metrics are simply better.

Claim two: value requires more than one person or workflow. Lakshna passes decisively — field operations is a coordination product, worthless to a single user. Kalpavriksh passes only partially: Flow genuinely delivers value through one engineer's pipelines, so its multi-person requirement is about durability, not value creation. Conflating the two pushes a team toward collaboration features when the remedy is succession and template reuse.

Claim three: the renewal decision is made by someone who can be shown evidence. Both pass, which is why both benefit from function-level breakdowns: such a breakdown is as much an argument for the sponsor as a diagnostic for the vendor.

Claim four: the contract period leaves time to act on early signals. Lakshna's annual contracts give nine months of runway; Kalpavriksh's monthly consumption billing gives far less, which changes the design. A monthly lagging score is nearly worthless to Jyotika; a real-time alert on authorship or burn-down deviation is not.

The idea is actively misleading in one common case. When a product is mandated top-down as an enterprise standard, adoption metrics stop measuring value and start measuring compliance; Konkan's shift tap is the specimen. In mandated deployments the honest metrics are outcomes owned jointly with the customer — schedule adherence, time to close an inspection — because any usage metric will be gamed, without malice, by people obeying an instruction.

5. Hard Edges

Multi-product. When Lakshna launched Lakshna Plan alongside Field, the rollup broke quietly: a supervisor holding both licences counted twice in provisioned seats, and cross-product activation had no agreed meaning. Mature companies resolve this with a canonical person identity spanning products and a rule that account health is the minimum, not the mean, across products bought. Most say they do this; a majority discover at audit that their identity graph merges on work email, which fails the moment a customer changes domain.

Two-sided and platform. At Laari Exchange, a B2B freight marketplace, an account's health is partly a function of the other side's liquidity in its lane. A Nagpur fleet operator with excellent engagement and no matched loads is not unhealthy; it is unserved. Treating supply-side health as an account attribute rather than a market attribute aims interventions at the wrong party.

Regulated. Lalima, supervised by the RBI and operating under account-aggregator rules, restricts what telemetry Kalpavriksh may retain about named individuals, and India's data-protection regime has sharpened that constraint sector-wide. Per-user metrics may be contractually unavailable in precisely the accounts that matter most. The workaround is role-level aggregation agreed in the data-processing addendum — so metric design must happen before the deal closes, not after.

Hardware plus software. Jugnu Devices sells cold-chain sensors with a monitoring subscription; the unit of adoption is the installed, reporting device. An account with 900 devices of which 210 have gone dark has a churn problem no software metric shows, because the software looks fine to the humans still watching the 690. Installed-base telemetry belongs in the score with real weight.

AI-native. Kolam AI, which reviews vendor contracts and prices per document, learned that volume and value can move in opposite directions: usage was highest where the model was worst, because reviewers re-ran documents. The load-bearing metric was acceptance — the share of generated suggestions a human kept — and no seat or volume metric contains it.

At the organisational seams, the recurring failure is definitional drift: sales counts contracts, finance counts invoiced legal entities, product counts tenants, customer success counts relationships spanning several of each. What mature companies actually do, as against what their charters claim, is nominate one system of record — nearly always the CRM, where money is booked — and require every other system to carry its identifier as a foreign key. Unglamorous, two quarters of work, and the highest-leverage investment in B2B measurement there is.

6. Where Expertise Shows

Distinguishing depth, breadth and durability

Three things travel under the word adoption: how intensely a user uses the product, how many functions use it at all, and how resistant that use is to one person leaving. Konkan was deep and narrow; Kartavya shallow and broad. The tell is an account team that cannot say which of the three worries them — they say a customer is "not very engaged," and pressing produces a pause. The obvious reading, that all three collapse into one score, is wrong: they respond to different interventions — depth to training, breadth to sponsorship, durability to enablement.

Reading the denominator before the ratio

B2B ratios have unstable denominators: provisioned users move when a customer's HR system syncs, seats at renewal, tenants when a plant onboards. Read the denominator series before the ratio, because a rising rate produced by a shrinking denominator — a customer deprovisioning inactive staff — is the same arithmetic as improvement and the opposite signal.

Knowing which metric is a lead and which is a lag

Seat utilisation is a lag; breadth of first-time use across functions is a lead. The tell is a score whose components all move together in the last sixty days before churn: composed of lagging indicators, it describes a fire rather than predicting one. The obvious reading — that a score correlating strongly with churn must be good — is wrong, because contemporaneous correlation is worthless for action.

Refusing to average across heterogeneous accounts

A platform-wide activation rate across accounts spanning ₹8 lakh to ₹4 crore makes the largest customers statistically invisible. Report revenue-weighted and logo-weighted figures side by side and treat divergence as the finding, not noise: when they diverge, the product works for one size of customer and not another — a segmentation problem masquerading as a metrics problem.

Treating the activation definition as perishable

A definition validated on last year's renewals describes last year's product sold to last year's customer mix. The sign of staleness is a customer-success team quietly keeping a private spreadsheet that overrides the official score — not insubordination but re-validation arriving through the wrong channel, and the response is to read it, not ban it.

Separating the score from the intervention

A good score ranks accounts by risk; it does not say what to do. Teams that choose components because they map to existing playbooks get a score that only sees problems it already knows how to fix. The tell is a score that never flags an account for a reason nobody has a playbook for — which in a healthy book should happen twice a quarter.

Watching for reverse causality in learned scores

Support tickets are the classic contaminant. A model trained on churn learns that ticket volume predicts it, then ranks a vocal, loyal account as at-risk while ignoring the silent one that has stopped caring. The diagnostic: which features would the model lose if restricted to behaviour the customer considers a sign of investment?

Distinguishing the sponsor's view from the user's

Renewals are signed by people who often do not use the product. An account can have excellent user metrics and a sponsor who has seen no evidence of return, or wretched metrics and a sponsor personally committed to the programme. The tell is a score with no field for whether the economic buyer has seen outcome evidence in ninety days — a variable that in most B2B books predicts renewal as well as anything behavioural.

7. How It Differs by Product Type and Stage

Across consumer and B2B the difference is structural, not one of degree: in consumer products payer, user and beneficiary are one person, the stack collapses to one layer, and activation is a single individual event. Between mid-market and enterprise the difference is real but mostly concerns the number of independent adoption decisions inside one contract — Lakshna's mid-market accounts behave like one organism, its 1,400-seat accounts like a federation of five. Platforms add liquidity dependency; hardware adds an installed base that fails silently; AI adds an acceptance-quality dimension that volume inverts.

The difference is overstated between vertical and horizontal software: the architecture is identical, and only the obviousness of the workflow denominator changes. A vertical product knows its unit is an inspection or a claim; a horizontal product must work to find one — but both are better off having found it.

Stage changes the honest answer more than most admit. Below roughly thirty accounts no health score is justified: a founder reading every account by hand outperforms any model. From thirty to a few hundred, hand-weighted scores with auditable components are right, because the organisation needs to argue about the weights and learn what it believes. Above that, learned models beat hand weights on ranking accuracy at the cost of explainability, which is why mature companies run both and investigate disagreements. The failure at each transition is identical: carrying the previous stage's instrument past the point where its assumptions hold.

8. Three Accounts, Worked

One: the rescue at Lakshna. After Konkan, Latika rebuilt the score around function coverage rather than user averages, with four components: breadth (share of contracted functions with a core action each week), depth (median core actions per active user), durability (share of workflows configured by more than one administrator) and sponsor evidence (a dated flag for the last business review with outcome data). The amber band — larger in count, second in expected loss — was where product rather than customer success could act, because amber accounts failed on breadth, and breadth is an onboarding and packaging problem.

Two: the small account that mattered. Kartavya Lending's ₹40 lakh made it unremarkable on revenue and exceptional on durability: six authors, three teams, concentration 0.206, new pipelines forked rather than written from scratch. Kalpavriksh had been ranking expansion prospects by current spend; re-ranked by author breadth, Kartavya entered the top decile, and over the next year its consumption grew 2.6 times to ₹1.04 crore while Lalima's fell 38 percent. In consumption businesses, the number of people who can create demand forecasts next year's revenue better than this year's revenue does.

Three: the failure at Kolam AI, and the recovery. Kolam's founders, arriving from seat-licensed SaaS, imported the playbook whole: activation was ten documents reviewed within thirty days, and the health score weighted document volume at 45 percent. Jasol Cements, processing over 4,000 documents a month, topped every leaderboard for two quarters and gave notice in the third. The post-mortem found an acceptance rate of 9 percent: reviewers ran documents through Kolam, rejected nearly everything and re-drafted manually, because for cement-sector procurement contracts the model had learned the wrong clause distribution. Volume was measuring failure. The recovery took three quarters and was not primarily analytical. Kolam had to instrument suggestion-level accept, edit and reject events it had never captured, so fourteen months of history could not be back-filled and the new score had no validation set until renewals accumulated; 200 human-graded documents a week served as the bridge. Net revenue retention, down to 91 percent, reached 109 percent four quarters later. The instructive cost was not the churned account but a year of roadmap spent making a product faster when the problem was that it was wrong.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Warnings

Compliance mistaken for adoption. Early sign: a usage metric with implausibly low variance across accounts. Diagnostic: what would this number do if the customer's policy changed but their opinion of us did not? Caught late, the score is green at the moment of loss.

Tenant–account mismatch. Early sign: account counts differing between the CRM and product analytics by more than a few percent. Diagnostic: count your three largest customers in both systems by hand. Late cost: every per-account metric silently wrong, and a year of decisions made on them.

Single-builder concentration. Early sign: usage growth with flat or falling author counts. Diagnostic: what share of this account's value comes from its largest contributor, and who is second? Late cost: a step-function revenue drop with no warning, as at Lalima.

Stale activation definitions. Early sign: shadow spreadsheets in customer success. Diagnostic: when was this threshold last tested against renewal outcomes, on which cohort? Late cost: slow, expensive misallocation of intervention capacity.

Volume as a proxy for value in AI and consumption products. Early sign: usage rising while qualitative feedback sours. Diagnostic: what fraction of the work we did was kept? Late cost: Kolam's roadmap year spent on the wrong axis.

10. Genuine Disagreements

Should the North Star be an account metric or a user metric? The account camp argues that money renews at the account, that user metrics can rise while accounts die, and that every function outside product already thinks in accounts. The user camp argues that account metrics are non-actionable for feature teams, move too slowly to steer a roadmap, and that in bottom-up products expansion is downstream of individual value moments. The account camp fails if renewals stop being sales-mediated; the user camp fails if individual value moments do not aggregate into account outcomes in coordination products — which Konkan suggests they sometimes do not.

Hand-weighted or learned health scores? The hand-weighted case rests on auditability and organisational learning: a weight is a belief that can be argued with, and a manager acts on a score they can explain. The learned case rests on ranking accuracy, usually measurably better. The hand case fails if intervention capacity is the binding constraint and ranking is all that matters; the learned case fails wherever reverse causality contaminates features.

Does activation exist at all for consumption products? One camp holds it is a category error outside seat models — there is only usage depth and commitment burn-down, and any threshold is arbitrary. The other holds that Kalpavriksh's second-builder rule is a genuine activation event with predictive content. This is unresolved, and the evidence for consumption-product thresholds is thinner than the confidence with which they are asserted.

How much per-user telemetry is legitimate in enterprise accounts? The measurement camp holds that individual data is necessary to help the customer succeed; the restraint camp holds that vendors should not build surveillance infrastructure over a customer's employees, and that role-level aggregation loses little. This one is drifting toward restraint on regulatory momentum rather than argument.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Mastery shows in three habits. Before reading any B2B number, the expert asks which of the four units it is counted in and what its denominator did last quarter — ten seconds, and it catches most errors. They report distributions and segments by default, having learned that the mean of a bimodal population is a claim about nobody. And they hold definitions loosely but governance tightly: they will change a threshold on evidence, and will not let two teams count accounts two ways. Someone who has merely studied this can recite accounts, seats, users and activation; someone who has internalised it spends their energy on identity plumbing and the aggregation rule, because that is where the errors live.

12. What They Decided

Jyotika stopped treating consumption as the unit of health. Kalpavriksh added two attributes to every account review — distinct pipeline authors in the trailing quarter, and author concentration — and made a second builder within ninety days the explicit goal of onboarding, with templates and an enablement workshop built to serve it. She refused to add a login-based engagement metric: Flow's humans were not supposed to be in the product daily, and rewarding that would have distorted the roadmap. In a consumption business the durable asset is the number of people inside the customer who can create demand, and that, not revenue, was what she owed the board a forecast on.

Latika kept the health score but changed what it was made of: function coverage in place of user averages, a durability component, a dated sponsor-evidence flag, and the shift tap removed from the core-action definition entirely. She also published old and new scores side by side for two quarters, so the organisation could see which accounts moved and argue about why rather than be handed an instrument by fiat. Konkan was not saved; eleven of the forty-two red accounts the new score surfaced were, which at an average of ₹19 lakh each roughly paid for the work in its first year.

Discussion questions. First: Lakshna's revised score requires a dated sponsor conversation — a human-entered field in an otherwise behavioural instrument. When does it improve the score, and when does it become a compliance ritual of the kind the shift tap turned out to be? Second: an account could centralise pipeline authorship for sound engineering reasons. How would you separate healthy centralisation from key-person risk using data Kalpavriksh already has? Third: how should a public metric you have come to believe is wrong be retired, and who owns that decision?

13. Going Deeper

  1. North Star metric — forces the account-level versus user-level choice; turns section 10's argument into a decision.
  2. SaaS metrics: ARR, MRR, churn, NRR — the financial layer these metrics must predict; supplies the test that separates a real activation bar from a decorative one.
  3. Driving adoption inside the account — the intervention side of everything diagnosed here.
  4. Account health scores — composition, weighting and calibration of the instrument Latika rebuilt; unlocks triage beyond hand-reading.
  5. What makes a good metric — sensitivity, gameability, actionability; makes rejecting the shift tap defensible.
  6. Vanity vs actionable metrics — the distinction Kolam's document volume violated; asks what decision a number changes.
  7. GAME framework — ties each metric to an owner, a cadence and a decision; unlocks metric governance.
  8. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — where account metrics attach to commercial levers; unlocks Kartavya-style expansion forecasting.
  9. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — the denominator discipline; unlocks correct reading of activation rates on moving bases.
  10. Attention, transaction, productivity games — the game a product plays determines which metrics can be right; explains the mandated-deployment exception.

Aayam Retail Cloud: Which Number Goes on the Board Slide?

Bengaluru, September 2026. Three colleagues describe the same company with three different numbers. One of them has to go on a slide by the thirtieth.

1. Thursday evening, HSR Layout

At about seven on the evening of Thursday, 10 September 2026, Shruti Kulkarni closed a spreadsheet she had been staring at since lunch and wrote three lines on the whiteboard of a small meeting room on the third floor of Aayam Retail Cloud's office in HSR Layout, Bengaluru. The lines read: 96 accounts. 1.45 lakh paid seats. 3.4 lakh monthly app users. Under them she wrote a fourth line, and then rubbed it out twice before leaving it: which one do we manage?

Shruti was vice-president of product. On 30 September the board would review the operating plan for the second half of the financial year, and Rajat Menon, the co-founder and chief executive, had asked her for one thing: a single product metric of record that the whole company would be judged on, with the reporting to support it. He had been clear about why. In the previous four quarters the product organisation had optimised app engagement, sales had optimised seat counts, customer success had optimised renewal conversations, and all three had reported a good year while net revenue retention came in at 101 per cent. Five accounts had churned. All five, when Shruti went back to look, had healthy monthly user numbers on the day they gave notice.

2. The company

Aayam Retail Cloud was founded in 2018 by Rajat Menon and Sandeep Barua, both formerly of Infosys, to sell what Indian retail had been running on paper: a store-operations platform. Its modules covered daily task lists for store staff, planogram and display compliance through photographs, opening and closing checklists, cold-chain temperature logs, stock-count audits, and since 2025 a catalogue-sync module for chains selling on ONDC-connected apps and on the marketplaces. It was sold to chains, not to single shops, on annual contracts at ₹230 to ₹380 per seat per month depending on module mix.

By September 2026 it had 96 paying accounts and ₹41 crore of annual recurring revenue. Its customers were supermarket chains in Maharashtra and Karnataka, two pharmacy chains, an apparel group with 410 outlets, a quick-service restaurant franchisor, a spectacles retailer, and three fuel-station operators. Its largest account was in the Gulf: Al Barakah Markets, a grocery chain headquartered in Dubai with 128 stores across the Emirates and Oman, worth ₹3.2 crore a year and up for renewal in January 2027.

The market around it was moving quickly in ways that helped and hurt. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — had trained Indian shoppers to expect ten-minute delivery, which pushed physical chains to run tighter store operations and made Aayam's pitch easier. Reliance Retail and the Tata group ran their own in-house systems, so the top of the market was closed. Flipkart and Meesho had pulled a slice of apparel demand away from Aayam's mid-sized apparel customers, which meant those customers were cutting costs. Indian SaaS peers such as Zoho and Freshworks set the benchmark investors used for capital efficiency, and Aayam's investors quoted them often. GST e-invoicing had made the audit module a compliance necessity rather than a nice-to-have, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had forced a redesign of how store-staff photographs were stored and retained.

One operational fact about Indian retail shaped everything Shruti was trying to measure. In most of Aayam's customers, a store did not give each employee a device. A store had one or two Android tablets on a counter, shared by six to fourteen staff across shifts, plus the manager's own phone. Seats were bought per staff member because that was how Aayam priced, but the person behind a login was frequently not the person who had been issued it, and temporary festival-season staff logged in on whatever tablet was free.

3. The situation

The trigger had been a Monday call in August. Farida Merchant, who led customer success from Singapore and carried 41 of the 96 accounts, said she believed three accounts were in trouble and could not prove it to anyone's satisfaction. Her evidence was anecdotal and good: at one pharmacy chain the regional operations head had stopped attending the monthly review; at Al Barakah, the Dubai team had begun asking for data exports, which in Farida's experience was what customers did when they were evaluating a replacement.

Priyanka Rao, the data scientist in Toronto, had built a health score in 2025 out of eleven signals, most of them variants of login frequency. Shruti had asked her in August to check it against what had actually happened. Priyanka's answer, sent at 3 a.m. India time, was uncomfortable: of the eleven accounts the score had marked red ninety days before their renewal, two had churned; of the five accounts that did churn, the score had flagged two. She added a line Shruti kept returning to: "The score cannot see accounts, only logins. Two of the five churns are recorded in our system as separate accounts per region, so the churn shows up as partial."

Katharina Böhm in Berlin had a proposal ready: redesign first-run onboarding so that a new store user reached a completed task within four minutes. Devansh Chopra in New Jersey, opening the North American market with two pilot logos, wanted seat counts on the board slide, because his quota and his commission were denominated in seats and he did not want the company reporting a number he was not paid on.

4. The people

Shruti Kulkarni, vice-president of product, Bengaluru. Wants a metric that tells her team what to build on Monday and that survives contact with the board. Suspects the engagement number she has been reporting for two years is the reason nobody saw the five churns coming.

Rajat Menon, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants one number, defensible in front of investors who read it against Zoho and Freshworks. His instinct favours the 3.4 lakh user figure because it is large and grows; he has also said, privately, that he never wants to be surprised by a churn again.

Farida Merchant, customer-success lead, Singapore. Wants a ranked worklist of accounts by risk, delivered every Monday morning her time, that she can trust enough to reallocate her four customer-success managers against.

Devansh Chopra, head of sales, New Jersey. Wants seats, for reasons of compensation and of simplicity. Points out, not unreasonably, that Aayam's price list is per seat, so a metric that ignores seats is a metric divorced from revenue.

Priyanka Rao, data scientist, Toronto. Wants six weeks of engineering time from the Pune team to fix the account hierarchy and stamp an account identifier on every event before she rebuilds anything. Has said she will not put her name on a second score built on the current data.

The same 96 accounts, in the same week, can be described as 3.4 lakh users growing at 94 per cent, as 70 per cent seat activation, or as 38 activated accounts out of 96. None of the three is false. They imply completely different plans for the next two quarters.

6. The options

Option A — keep the engagement metric and fix onboarding. Make monthly active store users the metric of record, fund Katharina's four-minute-to-first-task redesign, and hold seats and accounts as secondary reporting. Upside: nothing to rebuild, the number is large and rising, the whole company already understands it, and the onboarding work is genuinely good work. Cost: this is the metric that was in place while five accounts churned unnoticed, and it cannot distinguish Al Barakah from Sahyadri Supermarts, which is the distinction that matters most in the next hundred days.

Option B — make account activation the metric of record. Adopt the strict test as the company metric, report it alongside activated ARR, retire monthly app users from board reporting, and give Priyanka the six weeks of Pune engineering time to model the account hierarchy and stamp account identifiers on events. Farida gets a ranked Monday worklist. Upside: it is the only lens in Exhibit 3 that would have flagged Al Barakah and Konkan Fuels; it puts product and customer success on the same number; it is the number that predicts renewal. Cost: the headline falls from 3.4 lakh to 38, which Rajat will have to explain to investors; six weeks of engineering capacity comes out of the ONDC catalogue module; and the metric moves slowly, so a product team optimising it weekly will feel little feedback.

Option C — make seat activation the metric of record. Adopt activated seats as a share of paid seats, currently 70 per cent against assigned and 57 per cent against sold. Upside: it maps directly onto the price list, aligns Devansh's quota with the company metric, needs no hierarchy project, and the sold-versus-assigned gap is a real and large commercial opportunity — 27,000 unassigned seats across the portfolio. Cost: in Indian retail a seat is a fiction. Shared tablets mean the denominator is an administrative artefact; the metric improves whenever a customer's administrator does a bulk assignment; and it is blind to the manager-reach problem, which is the signal that distinguishes the accounts that renew.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, rank the eight accounts by risk of non-renewal and state the evidence for your top three. Where does Al Barakah sit, and why does it look healthy on some columns?

2. What exactly does each of Aayam's three numbers measure, and for each, name one decision it is well suited to informing and one it is not?

3. Priyanka's health score caught two of five churns. Was the problem the model, the signals, or the data on which accounts exist? What would you check first?

4. Which option should Shruti take to the board on 30 September, and what would she say when Rajat asks why the headline number just fell from 3.4 lakh to 38?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a distinction that consumer-product intuition erases: in a business that sells to organisations, the unit of money, the unit of entitlement and the unit of behaviour are three different things. The account signs, pays and churns. The seat is a licence that may sit unassigned. The user is a person — and at Aayam, thanks to shared tablets and festival staffing, not even a stable person. A measurement system earns its keep by keeping the three separate and then connecting them, so that behaviour at the bottom explains money at the top.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It recognises that the metric of record must be denominated in the unit of the decision the company most fears getting wrong — here, renewal, which is an account-level event. It treats activation per account as a threshold on several dimensions at once (breadth of adoption, depth of workflow completion, reach into the people who decide, sustained over weeks), not as a single event or a single percentage. And it declares denominators: 89 per cent breadth at Drishti Opticals is computed on 300 assigned seats out of 520 sold, and is therefore a statement about one enthusiastic region.

One defensible path is Option B, staged, with one piece of Option C carried inside it. Shruti takes account activation to the board as the metric of record and reports it in two forms — count of accounts and share of ARR — because the first keeps distribution visible and the second speaks the board's language. She retires monthly app users from the board slide but keeps it as an operational input, since it is the earliest signal product has and the loss of a leading indicator is a real cost. She preserves the seat insight by adding assigned-seat share as a named input metric owned by Farida, which captures the 27,000-seat commercial gap that Devansh legitimately cares about without letting a gameable number become the company's goal. She funds Priyanka's six weeks, on the argument that without an account identifier on every event no version of this system can work, and accepts the delay to the ONDC module. And she makes one concrete near-term commitment: manager reach at Al Barakah, currently one, is the target for the next six weeks, because the account renews in January and no amount of store-level engagement will save a renewal that no decision-maker has a reason to defend.

The reasoning for choosing B over A is that A is the status quo that produced five unseen churns; the reasoning for choosing B over C is that C measures an artefact of Indian retail staffing rather than adoption. The honest cost of B is the one Rajat will feel on 30 September: a truer number is a smaller number, and the first board meeting after you start measuring properly is always the worst one.

Pune — 3 September 2026

1. A Renewal Nobody Saw Coming

Meher Rawal had built her Tuesday board update around one number, and by Monday night that number no longer meant what she thought it meant. Meher was VP of Product at Mool Systems, a Pune-based maker of MoolBoard, a work-planning tool sold to mid-market Indian companies — logistics firms, contract manufacturers, professional-services shops — for planning projects and tracking deadlines across departments. Mool's dashboard showed monthly active users up 14 percent quarter over quarter, a healthy story for a Series B company chasing its next round. But that morning, Ishaan Bhatt, her customer-success lead in Chennai, flagged that Parisar Logistics — a 240-seat account worth ₹86 lakh in annual recurring revenue, Mool's fourth-largest customer — had quietly stopped answering renewal emails.

The contradiction was the problem. Mool's user-growth number was rising because Parisar's warehouse-operations team, forty new hires onboarded that quarter, had logged in at least once. Almost none had built a project board, assigned a task, or invited a colleague — the behaviours Mool's own research linked to customers staying past year one. Parisar's finance team, meanwhile, was the account's heaviest user by login count, using MoolBoard as a glorified to-do list for a workflow it had run in Excel for a decade. Meher's dashboard counted logins per person and called it health; it could not say whether Parisar as a company was getting value, only whether some individual inside it had opened the app. She had six weeks before the renewal conversation and a board expecting an answer grounded in more than a login count. The real decision was what Mool should count as a unit of success — account, seat, or person — and what "activated" should mean when the customer paying the bill is an organisation, not an individual.

2. The Idea: Measuring the Buyer, Not the User

In a consumer product, the person who signs up, uses the product, and determines whether the company survives is one individual. In a B2B product those roles split apart. The company that pays — the account — is not the people who log in, and the people who log in are not uniformly the people whose adoption determines whether the deal renews. B2B product metrics is the practice of measuring value creation at the level of the paying organisation, not just the individual user, by tracking four distinct units — the account, the seats purchased within it, the users provisioned against those seats, and the subset who reach meaningful activation — and asking not "did someone log in" but "did the account, as a whole, reach the pattern of use that predicts renewal and expansion."

The discipline did not arrive as a single named invention the way the Net Promoter Score did. It crystallised through the 2010s as SaaS matured into a distinct business model, with writers such as David Skok at Matrix Partners and the "customer success" movement that grew up around firms like Gainsight from roughly 2013 arguing that metrics consumer apps had popularised — daily active users, session length — were dangerously incomplete for a business sold account-by-account, on annual contracts. The sentence Meher could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: we don't have a user-adoption problem or a company-adoption problem until we know which one we have, and each needs a different fix.

3. The Mechanics: Four Layers, One Funnel

The mechanics start with a hierarchy, and practitioners often skip the first step because it feels too obvious: define the account. An account is the commercial entity that signs the contract and receives one invoice — for Mool, Parisar Logistics as a single legal customer, not each regional depot. Inside that account sit seats: the named licences the contract entitles it to provision, set at sale time and renegotiated at renewal. Parisar had bought 240. Below seats sit users: the individuals to whom a Parisar administrator has assigned a licence and login — 210 of 240 seats, leaving thirty unassigned, itself a signal worth watching, since unused seats are revenue already being paid for without value extracted.

The step most often left implicit is next: not every provisioned user is active, and not every active user is activated, and "activated" must be decided deliberately rather than inherited from a consumer template. Activation is the specific, observable action or short sequence that a product team has determined — usually through cohort analysis of customers who did versus did not renew — predicts durable value. Mool's data team found that users who, within fourteen days, created one project board and invited two teammates were retained at twice the rate, six months later, of users who merely logged in. That became MoolBoard's activation definition: not a login, a specific pair of actions within a window.

The final and most consequential step is aggregation: rolling individual activation into an account-level score, because an account does not have "an activation rate" the way one user does — it has a distribution, and the business decision (renew, expand, intervene) depends on that shape, not the average alone. This is where teams new to B2B metrics stumble, because averaging hides exactly the failure Meher faced: a healthy mean masking one department that never adopted at all.

4. Working the Numbers

Meher asked Kabir Suri, Mool's Bengaluru-based data analyst, to pull the account-level breakdown for Parisar rather than the platform-wide average. Parisar had 210 provisioned users. Of those, 149 had logged in at least once in the trailing thirty days — a monthly-active-user rate of 71 percent, the number that made Mool's aggregate dashboard look healthy. Applying the fourteen-day activation rule — one board created, two teammates invited — only 61 of 210 qualified as activated. Account-level activation rate: 61 ÷ 210 = 29 percent.

The department breakdown explained the renewal risk. Of the 61 activated users, 52 sat in two departments — planning and finance, both early pilot users from the original sale eighteen months earlier. Of forty newly hired warehouse-operations staff, only 4 had activated; the other 36 logged in once, during onboarding, and never returned. Warehouse operations was also the function generating the manual scheduling errors that had motivated the original purchase. A platform-wide MAU of 71 percent told Meher nothing about this; a 29 percent activation rate, sliced by department, told her exactly where the deal was at risk.

Now change one input. Suppose Mool tightened its activation definition after Kabir found the two-invite threshold too weak — accounts meeting it still churned at 18 percent within a year, while accounts requiring three invites and one board with five-plus tasks churned at only 6 percent. Re-run Parisar under the stricter rule: activated users fall from 61 to 23, and activation drops from 29 percent to 11 percent. The second pass changes the decision, not just the number. At 29 percent, a training nudge to warehouse operations might suffice. At 11 percent, with finance and planning barely clearing the bar too, the honest read is one healthy pocket and three departments the product hasn't reached — an executive-sponsor conversation, not a training email.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Sit With

Seats are a commercial fact, not an adoption fact

Seat count shows what an account bought, useful for expansion forecasting, but says nothing about use. Buying 240 seats and provisioning 210 is a purchasing decision; whether those 210 people do anything with the product is a separate question seat data cannot answer.

"User" is ambiguous until you specify provisioned, logged-in, or activated

Teams routinely say "we have 210 users" and mean three different things — sales means provisioned, the dashboard means logged-in-recently, customer success means activated. A definition that does not name which one it measures will be misread by someone in the room.

Account-level averages hide department-level failure

Parisar is the canonical trap: a respectable average conceals one department at zero. A health score built only on an aggregate, without a distributional view across departments, misses exactly the failures that predict churn — the unhappy department is rarely the one running the review.

Activation definitions expire and must be re-validated

Behaviours that predicted retention eighteen months ago may not predict it today, as products add features and customer mix shifts. Mool's two-invite rule proving too weak once more churn data accumulated shows a definition is a hypothesis to test against renewal outcomes, not a rule set once and forgotten.

Activation, habitual use and expansion are three different signals

A user can clear an activation threshold once and never return; a team can use a product habitually and narrowly, never expanding to new seats. Collapsing these related but distinct signals into one composite score without understanding each invites the confusion that plagued Parisar's dashboard.

Who owns the threshold matters as much as what it is

A definition set unilaterally by product, without customer success (who see what correlates with renewals) or sales (who know what was promised), tends to measure what is easy to instrument rather than what the business needs to know.

These metrics cannot tell you why a department has not adopted

Knowing warehouse operations activated at 10 percent diagnoses where, not why. It cannot distinguish a training gap, a workflow mismatch, an unconvinced manager, or a genuine product gap — that needs the qualitative work of talking to the account, which the metric can only prompt, not replace.

Ask whose definition it is, and when it was last checked against renewals

A newcomer inheriting a health score should ask who set the thresholds, what validated them, how recently, and whether the score is reported by account and department or only as a platform-wide blend that would hide a Parisar-shaped problem.

6. How This Differs Across Products and Stages

In a consumer product, buyer and user are one person, so activation is single-layer — did this individual reach value — and the apparatus of accounts and seats does not exist. In a marketplace, there are two sides, supply and demand, each with its own activation definition, and health depends on both clearing their bar in roughly matched proportion. B2B sits apart from both because payer and user are structurally different populations, and a marketplace's two-sided problem becomes, in B2B, a many-sided one — a single account can contain several departments, each behaving like its own mini-market for adoption, as Parisar shows.

Stage matters too. An early-stage company with twenty accounts can review every account's activation by hand, as Meher's predecessor did monthly when Mool had thirty customers. At Mool's current size, roughly 300 accounts, that no longer scales — which is why health scores exist: a codified, weighted blend of account-level activation, breadth across departments, and seat utilisation, calculated automatically so Ishaan's team can triage which accounts need a human look this week. The risk at scale is that codification drifts from the truth manual review used to catch, so the score itself needs periodic revalidation against actual renewal outcomes, not just at founding.

7. Common Mistakes

Mistaking login for activation. Symptom: a dashboard that looks healthy right up until a renewal is lost. Error: treating "opened the app" as a proxy for value received, when the two are only loosely correlated. Cheapest diagnostic: pull activation-defined behaviour for accounts that churned last two quarters and check whether login rate would have predicted it — usually it would not.

Reporting only the platform-wide average. Symptom: a metric that never explains any single account's behaviour. Error: averaging across accounts of wildly different size and maturity, which guarantees no individual story is visible. Cheapest diagnostic: check your three largest accounts against the average individually — if it is wrong for two of three, it is not a decision-grade metric.

Setting a threshold once and never revisiting it. Symptom: a health score customer success has quietly stopped trusting and overrides with gut feel. Error: treating the original cohort analysis as permanent truth rather than a hypothesis tied to a product version and customer mix. Cheapest diagnostic: correlate the current activation flag against renewals from the last two quarters; a weakened correlation means the definition is stale.

Counting seats sold as a proxy for value delivered. Symptom: a growth story built on expansion revenue that reverses at renewal. Error: conflating a commercial transaction with product adoption. Cheapest diagnostic: track seat-utilisation rate — provisioned over purchased, activated over provisioned — alongside seat count, not instead of it.

8. What Good Looks Like

Six months later, Rudra Composites — a smaller, 60-seat Mool account in Coimbatore — came up for renewal, and Ishaan's team handled it the way Meher now wanted every account handled. The dashboard showed 52 of 60 seats provisioned, 44 activated under the stricter three-invite rule, and activation broken out by department: procurement at 90 percent, production planning at 25 percent. Rather than report one comforting blend, Ishaan flagged production planning to the account champion eight weeks before renewal, ran a short workshop with that team, and re-measured. Activation there rose to 58 percent within a month. The renewal conversation was a routine confirmation, not a price negotiation, because the account team had already seen and fixed the problem the metric was built to reveal, department by department, before it became a churn event.

9. What Meher Decided

Meher went into the Parisar renewal with the department-level breakdown, not the platform average, and proposed something specific: a two-week guided rollout for warehouse operations, co-run with Parisar's own operations manager, targeting the stricter three-invite bar, with a follow-up review before the contract date. Shown their own adoption gap in concrete numbers rather than told to "use the product more," Parisar's leadership agreed to sponsor the rollout — the account renewed, and expanded by twenty seats six months later once warehouse operations caught up to planning and finance.

What Meher took from this, and pushed Mool's product organisation to adopt permanently, was a standing account-level dashboard — seats, provisioned users, activation by department, seat utilisation — reported alongside, not instead of, the platform-wide MAU number the board still liked. Next on her list was account health scoring: combining these four layers into one weighted signal that could triage 300 accounts a week without recreating the averaging trap that nearly cost her Parisar. Two questions worth sitting with: when your dashboard reports one company-wide number, whose activation is it actually describing — and if you cannot answer that in a sentence, what decision might it be quietly getting wrong?
